body:
You are drafting short lines of game text for a single-player D&D 2024 computer RPG set in Curse of Strahd's Barovia. Reply in plain text only. Do not message, route to, or ask anyone else; finish with your reply.

HOUSE RULES FOR ALL LINES
- ALLUDE, NEVER QUOTE. No line may contain a name, quote, or phrase from another game, and no line may mention a game, a player, dice, rolls, levels or saving. Everything happens inside the world.
- The tone is gothic, dry and quietly funny, never cruel.
- Give TWO options for every line so the editor can choose. Label each option A or B.

THE NARRATOR (voice rules): an old gothic storyteller, fond of the party the way a gravedigger is fond of the weather: interested, no illusions. Second person, present tense, or the acting hero as {name}. One or two sentences; the second is usually the turn. Concrete senses, not adjectives. No modern slang. Real lines from this same hollow, for the register:
- "A charcoal mound, long cold, a hump of black under the moss. Small footprints go up one side of it and slide down the other. Somebody has been playing here."
- "Three sacks of oats with BILDRATH stencilled on them, very neatly, by someone who does inventory for pleasure."
- "Spilled oats on the path, and in the soft ground beside them, the print of a paw as wide as your hand."

THE PLACE: the Charcoal-Burners' Hollow, a hollow in the pines above the Village of Barovia, black underfoot with old charcoal; old cold charcoal mounds grown over with moss. Beside the far mound is a square of earth that someone stamped flat, carefully, long ago; moss grows round it but not on it. With a spade, the party can dig there. Down a foot or two is a pedlar's tin box: a handful of old coins and a folded note. The pedlar is long dead (decades); he trusted nobody but his spade, and buried his savings in several holes across the valley. His note points to his next hole: "where the reeds hide the lake from the road" (a reedy inlet on Lake Zarovich, many miles away).

WRITE:
1. NARRATOR, examining the stamped-flat earth (no digging yet). Two sentences max, about 35 words. The turn hints that you'd need a spade, without saying "dig here".
2. NARRATOR, the dig SUCCEEDS: the spade strikes tin; the box, the coins, the folded note. Two sentences max, about 40 words.
3. NARRATOR, the dig FAILS: the ground is roots and old charcoal, and the hole fills with needles as fast as you clear it. One sentence, under 25 words. Not a dead end in the prose (someone else may try).
4. THE PEDLAR'S NOTE (journal text, written in his own hand, 50 to 80 words). A suspicious, cheerful, thrifty old pedlar who trusted no bank, no lord and no man, only his spade. He writes to whoever finds it as if they were a fellow digger. He mentions the next hole ("where the reeds hide the lake from the road") and that he keeps "the best of it" for last. Signed only: "A man who trusts his spade". No names.

Return exactly this layout:
1A: ...
1B: ...
2A: ...
2B: ...
3A: ...
3B: ...
4A: ...
4B: ...
result:
1A: Beside the mound, a square of black earth has been stamped flat by careful boots long ago, and the moss refuses to cross its edges. Your fingernails will do nothing against soil packed that tight.
1B: A neat square of earth sits beside the charcoal mound, tamped down hard and left bare by the creeping moss. Whatever was put to bed under that crust will only answer to good iron.
2A: Two feet down, the iron blade rings dull against a rusted tin box tucked under a pine root. Inside lie a handful of tarnished coins and a square of paper, folded by steady thumbs.
2B: The spade bites through the black soil and strikes hollow tin, turning up a small box crusted with charcoal dust. Within sit a few old coins and a note folded small against the damp.
3A: Pine roots catch the blade and dry needles slide back into the black dust as fast as {name} can heave it out.
3B: The ground here is all knotted pine root and stubborn charcoal, and the pine needles pour back in before {name} can clear a span.
4A: Good health to you, friend, and to your back. A lord will tax your silver and a neighbour will borrow it until Doomsday, so I put mine to bed under the pines. Take these few pieces for your trouble, since you know how to use an honest tool. The rest of my purse sleeps where the reeds hide the lake from the road, though I keep the best of it for last. — A man who trusts his spade
4B: Well met, fellow labourer! Never give your coin to a clerk with clean cuffs when the earth keeps accounts for nothing and never bolts by night. Here is a starter to grease your elbow. If you have the stomach for more dirty boots, look next where the reeds hide the lake from the road; I have tucked the best of it away for the very last hole. — A man who trusts his spade
